danish.title: Tiende bog (1812) — Kapitel 9
paragraphs: Indtil fyrst Andrej slog sig ned i Bogutjarovo, havde dets ejere altid været fraværende, og dets bønder var af en helt anden karakter end dem på Kahle Bjerge. De var forskellige i tale, klædedragt og sind. De kaldtes steppebønder. Den gamle fyrste havde værdsat dem for deres udholdenhed i arbejdet, når de kom til Kahle Bjerge for at hjælpe med høsten eller grave damme og grøfter, men han brød sig ikke om deres grovhed.

Fyrst Andrejs sidste ophold i Bogutjarovo, da han indførte hospitaler og skoler og nedsatte den afgift, bønderne måtte betale, havde ikke blødgjort deres sind, men tværtimod styrket de karaktertræk, den gamle fyrste kaldte grovhed. Forskellige dunkle rygter var altid i omløb blandt dem: snart at de alle skulle indskrives som kosakker, snart at der var en ny religion, de alle skulle omvendes til; så om en proklamation fra zaren og om eden til zar Paul i 1797 (i forbindelse med hvilken det hed sig, at friheden var blevet givet dem, men godsejerne havde standset den); så igen om Pjotr Fjodorovitjs tilbagevenden til tronen om syv år, da alt ville blive frit og så »enkelt«, at der slet ingen begrænsninger ville være. Rygtene om krigen med Bonaparte og hans invasion var i deres sind forbundet med de samme slags vage forestillinger om Antikrist, verdens ende og »den rene frihed.«

I omegnen af Bogutjarovo lå store landsbyer, der tilhørte kronen eller ejere, hvis livegne betalte afgift og kunne arbejde, hvor de ville. Der var meget få bosiddende godsejere i nabolaget og også meget få husfolk eller læsekyndige livegne, og i disse bønders liv var de hemmelighedsfulde understrømme i det russiske folks tilværelse — hvis årsager og mening er så gådefulde for samtidige — tydeligere og stærkere mærkbare end andetsteds. Et eksempel, der var indtruffet en snes år tidligere, var en bevægelse blandt bønderne for at udvandre til nogle ukendte »varme floder.« Hundreder af bønder, heriblandt Bogutjarovo-folkene, begyndte pludselig at sælge deres kvæg og drage af sted med hele familier mod sydøst. Som fugle, der trækker til et sted hinsides havet, strømmede disse mænd med deres hustruer og børn mod sydøst, til egne, hvor ingen af dem nogen sinde havde været. De drog af sted i karavaner, købte deres frihed én efter én eller flygtede og kørte eller gik mod de »varme floder.« Mange blev straffet, nogle sendt til Sibirien, mange døde af kulde og sult undervejs, mange vendte frivilligt tilbage, og bevægelsen døde ud af sig selv, lige så pludseligt som den var opstået, uden nogen tydelig årsag. Men sådanne understrømme fandtes stadig i folket og samlede nye kræfter, rede til at ytre sig lige så mærkeligt, uventet og samtidig simpelt, naturligt og kraftfuldt. Nu i 1812 var det for enhver, der levede i nær kontakt med disse mennesker, tydeligt, at disse understrømme virkede stærkt og nærmede sig et udbrud.

Alpatytj, der var nået til Bogutjarovo kort før den gamle fyrstes død, lagde mærke til en uro blandt bønderne, og at i modsætning til, hvad der skete i Kahle Bjerge-distriktet, hvor alle bønder inden for en radius af fyrre verst rejste bort og overlod deres landsbyer til kosakkernes hærgen, var bønderne i steppeegnen omkring Bogutjarovo ifølge rygternes sige i kontakt med franskmændene, modtog flyveblade fra dem, der gik fra hånd til hånd, og ikke flyttede. Han erfarede fra loyale husfolk, at bonden Karp, der havde stor indflydelse i landsbyens fællesskab og for nylig havde været borte som vognstyrer for en regeringstransport, var vendt tilbage med den nyhed, at kosakkerne ødelagde forladte landsbyer, men at franskmændene ikke skadede dem. Alpatytj vidste også, at den foregående dag havde en anden bonde fra landsbyen Visloukhovo, der var besat af franskmændene, bragt en proklamation fra en fransk general om, at ingen skade ville tilføjes indbyggerne, og at de ville få betaling for alt, der blev taget fra dem, hvis de blev. Som bevis herfor havde bonden medbragt fra Visloukhovo hundrede rubler i sedler (han vidste ikke, at de var falske), udbetalt som forskud for hø.

Vigtigere endnu erfarede Alpatytj, at den selv samme morgen, da han gav landsbyældsten ordre til at samle vogne til at flytte fyrstindens bagage fra Bogutjarovo, var der blevet holdt et landsbymøde, hvor det var besluttet ikke at flytte, men at vente. Alligevel var der ingen tid at spilde. Den femtende, den dag den gamle fyrste døde, havde marskalken insisteret på, at fyrstinde Marja straks måtte rejse, da det blev farligt. Han havde sagt hende, at han efter den sekstende ikke kunne stå inde for, hvad der ville ske. Om aftenen den dag, den gamle fyrste døde, tog marskalken af sted med løfte om at vende tilbage næste dag til begravelsen. Men det var han ude af stand til, for han modtog besked om, at franskmændene uventet var rykket frem, og han havde knap nok tid til at fjerne sin egen familie og sine ejendele fra sit gods.
I tredive år var Bogutjarovo blevet styret af landsbyældsten Dron, som den gamle fyrste kaldte ved kælenavnet »Drónusjka.«

Dron var en af de fysisk og mentalt kraftige bønder, der får store skæg, så snart de når den rette alder, og forbliver uforandrede, til de er tres eller halvfjerds, uden et gråt hår eller tabet af en tand, lige så ranke og stærke ved tres som ved tredive.

Kort efter udvandringen til de »varme floder«, hvori han havde deltaget ligesom de øvrige, blev Dron udnævnt til landsbyældste og opsynsmand for Bogutjarovo og havde siden udfyldt denne post upåklageligt i tre og tyve år. Bønderne frygtede ham mere end deres herre. Herrerne — både den gamle fyrste og den unge — og forvalteren respekterede ham og kaldte ham spøgende »ministeren.« Under hele sin tjenestetid havde Dron aldrig været beruset eller syg, aldrig efter søvnløse nætter eller de hårdeste opgaver havde han vist den mindste træthed, og skønt han ikke kunne læse, havde han aldrig glemt en eneste pengeregning eller antallet af tønder mel i nogen af de uendelige vognlæs, han solgte for fyrsten, eller en eneste neg af hele kornhøsten på en eneste tønde land af Bogutjarovos marker.

Alpatytj, der var ankommet fra det ødelagte Kahle Bjerge, sendte bud efter sin Dron den dag, fyrsten blev begravet, og sagde ham at skaffe tolv heste til fyrstindens vogne og atten vogne til de ting, der skulle flyttes fra Bogutjarovo. Skønt bønderne betalte afgift, mente Alpatytj, at det ikke ville volde vanskeligheder at opfylde denne ordre, for der var to hundrede og tredive husstande i arbejde i Bogutjarovo, og bønderne var velhavende. Men da Dron hørte ordren, slog han øjnene ned og forblev tavs. Alpatytj nævnte visse bønder, han kendte, og sagde ham, at han skulle tage vognene fra dem.

Dron svarede, at disse bønders heste var borte med transport. Alpatytj nævnte andre, men de havde heller ingen heste til rådighed ifølge Dron: nogle var i brug for staten, andre var for svage, og andre igen var døde af fodermangel. Det så ud til, at der slet ikke kunne skaffes heste, end ikke til vognene, endsige til transporten.

Alpatytj betragtede Dron skarpt og rynkede brynene. Ligesom Dron var en mønsterældste, havde Alpatytj heller ikke i tyve år forvaltet fyrstens godser forgæves. Han var en mønsterforvalter, der i højeste grad besad evnen til at ane behovene og instinkterne hos dem, han havde med at gøre. Et blik på Dron fik ham til straks at forstå, at hans svar ikke udtrykte hans personlige synspunkter, men den almene stemning i Bogutjarovos fællesskab, som ældsten allerede var blevet revet med af. Men han vidste også, at Dron, der havde erhvervet sig ejendom og var forhadt af fællesskabet, måtte vakle mellem de to lejre: herrernes og de livegnes. Han lagde mærke til denne vaklen i Drons blik og rykkede derfor tættere på med rynkede bryn.

»Hør nu her, Drónusjka,« sagde han. »Kom ikke med vrøvl til mig. Hans excellence fyrst Andrej gav mig selv ordre til at flytte alle folk væk og ikke lade dem blive hos fjenden, og der er også en ordre fra zaren om det. Enhver der bliver, er en forræder mod zaren. Har du forstået?«
»Jeg hører,« svarede Dron uden at løfte blikket.
Alpatytj var ikke tilfreds med dette svar.
»Nå, Dron, det ender galt!« sagde han og rystede på hovedet.
»Magten er i jeres hænder,« svarede Dron bedrøvet.

»Nå, Dron, drop det!« gentog Alpatytj, trak hånden fra brystet og pegede højtideligt mod gulvet ved Drons fødder. »Jeg kan se tværs igennem dig og tre alen ned i jorden under dig,« fortsatte han med blikket rettet mod gulvet foran Dron.
Dron blev forvirret, kastede et stjålent blik på Alpatytj og slog atter øjnene ned.

»Drop det vrøvl og sig til folk, at de skal gøre sig klar til at forlade deres hjem og drage til Moskva, og at de skal have vognene klar i morgen tidlig til fyrstindens ting. Og gå ikke til nogen forsamling selv, hører du?«
Dron faldt pludselig på knæ.
»Jakov Alpatytj, lad mig gå! Tag nøglerne fra mig og lad mig gå, for Kristi skyld!«

»Hold op med det!« råbte Alpatytj strengt. »Jeg ser tværs igennem dig og tre alen under dig,« gentog han, velvidende at hans dygtighed med biavl, hans viden om det rette tidspunkt for havresåning, og det faktum at han havde formået at bevare den gamle fyrstes gunst i tyve år, for længst havde skaffet ham ry for at være en troldmand, og at evnen til at se tre alen ned under en mand ansås for en troldmands egenskab.
Dron rejste sig og ville sige noget, men Alpatytj afbrød ham.
»Hvad har I fået i hovedet, hva? ... Hvad tænker I på, hva?«
»Hvad skal jeg stille op med folkene?« sagde Dron. »De er helt ude af sig selv; jeg har allerede sagt dem ...«
»'Sagt dem', det kan jeg tænke!« sagde Alpatytj. »Drikker de?« spurgte han brat.
»Helt ude af sig selv, Jakov Alpatytj; de har hentet endnu en tønde.«
»Nå, hør så her! Jeg tager til politimesteren, og du siger dem det, og at de skal holde op med det her, og at vognene skal stå klar.«
»Forstået.«

Alpatytj insisterede ikke yderligere. Han havde styret folk i lang tid og vidste, at den vigtigste måde at få dem til at adlyde var at vise ingen mistanke om, at de muligvis kunne lade være. Da han havde fået et underdanigt »forstået« ud af Dron, nøjedes Alpatytj med det, skønt han ikke blot tvivlede, men følte sig næsten sikker på, at vognene ikke ville blive stillet til rådighed uden hjælp fra tropper.

Og sådan gik det, for da aftenen kom, var ingen vogne stillet til rådighed. I landsbyen, uden for kroen, blev der holdt endnu et møde, som besluttede, at hestene skulle drives ud i skovene, og at vognene ikke skulle stilles til rådighed. Uden at sige noget om dette til fyrstinden lod Alpatytj sine egne ejendele tage af de vogne, der var kommet fra Kahle Bjerge, og lod disse heste gøre klar til fyrstindens vogne. Selv tog han til politimyndighederne.

english.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: Until Prince Andrew settled in Bogucharovo, its owners had always been absentees, and its peasants were quite different in character from those at Bald Hills. They differed in speech, dress, and temperament. They were called steppe peasants. The old prince approved of them for their hard work when they came to Bald Hills to help with the harvest or dig ponds and ditches, but he disliked them for their coarseness.

Prince Andrew's last stay at Bogucharovo, when he introduced hospitals and schools and reduced the rent the peasants had to pay, had not softened their nature but had on the contrary strengthened the very traits the old prince called coarseness. Various obscure rumors always circulated among them: sometimes a rumor that they would all be enrolled as Cossacks; sometimes talk of a new religion everyone would be converted to; then some proclamation of the Tsar's, or an oath to Tsar Paul in 1797 (in connection with which it was rumored that freedom had been granted but the landowners had suppressed it); then tales of Peter Fedorovich's return to the throne in seven years, when everything would be made free and so "simple" that there would be no rules at all. Rumors of the war with Bonaparte and his invasion were linked in their minds with the same vague ideas about the Antichrist, the end of the world, and "pure freedom."

In the area around Bogucharovo there were large villages belonging to the crown or to owners whose serfs paid rent and could work wherever they pleased. There were very few resident landlords nearby and also very few household or literate serfs, and in the lives of the peasantry in those parts, the mysterious undercurrents of Russian popular life—the causes and meaning of which are so baffling to outsiders—were more clearly and strongly evident than elsewhere. One example, which had occurred some twenty years before, was a movement among the peasants to emigrate to some unknown "warm rivers." Hundreds of peasants, including those from Bogucharovo, suddenly began selling their cattle and moving with their entire families toward the southeast. Like birds migrating beyond the sea, these men with their wives and children streamed toward the southeast, to places where none of them had ever been. They set off in caravans, bought their freedom one by one or ran away, and walked or drove toward the "warm rivers." Many were punished, some sent to Siberia, many died of cold and hunger on the road, many returned on their own, and the movement died down by itself just as it had sprung up, without apparent reason. But such undercurrents still existed among the people and gathered new force, ready to manifest themselves just as strangely, unexpectedly, and at the same time simply, naturally, and powerfully. Now in 1812, to anyone living in close contact with these people, it was apparent that these undercurrents were running strong and nearing an eruption.

Alpatych, who had reached Bogucharovo shortly before the old prince's death, noticed an agitation among the peasants, and that contrary to what was happening in the Bald Hills district—where over a radius of forty miles all the peasants were fleeing and leaving their villages to be ransacked by the Cossacks—the peasants in the steppe region around Bogucharovo were, it was rumored, in contact with the French, received leaflets from them that passed from hand to hand, and were not leaving. He learned from loyal household servants that the peasant Karp, who had great influence in the village commune and had recently been away driving a government transport, had returned with news that the Cossacks were destroying abandoned villages, but that the French didn't harm anyone. Alpatych also learned that the day before, another peasant had brought from the village of Visloukhovo, occupied by the French, a proclamation by a French general promising that no harm would come to the inhabitants and that they would be paid for anything taken. As proof, the peasant had brought from Visloukhovo a hundred rubles in banknotes (he didn't know they were counterfeit) paid to him in advance for hay.

More importantly, Alpatych learned that on the very morning he gave the village Elder orders to collect carts to move the princess's luggage from Bogucharovo, a village meeting had been held at which it was decided not to move but to wait. Yet there was no time to waste. On the fifteenth—the day of the old prince's death—the Marshal had insisted that Princess Mary leave immediately, as it was becoming dangerous. He told her that after the sixteenth he couldn't be responsible for what might happen. On the evening of the day the old prince died, the Marshal went away, promising to return the next day for the funeral. But he was unable to do so, because he received word that the French had unexpectedly advanced, and he barely had time to get his own family and possessions away from his estate.
For about thirty years, Bogucharovo had been managed by the village Elder, Dron, whom the old prince called by the pet name "Dronushka."

Dron was one of those physically and mentally vigorous peasants who grow big beards as soon as they come of age and go on unchanged until sixty or seventy, without a gray hair or the loss of a tooth, as straight and strong at sixty as at thirty.

Soon after the migration to the "warm rivers," in which he had taken part like the rest, Dron was made village Elder and overseer of Bogucharovo, and had filled that role irreproachably for twenty-three years. The peasants feared him more than they feared their master. The masters—both the old prince and the young—and the steward respected him and jokingly called him "the Minister." Throughout his entire service, Dron had never been drunk or sick; never, after sleepless nights or the hardest labor, had he shown the slightest fatigue; and though he could not read, he had never forgotten a single money account or the number of sacks of flour in any of the countless cartloads he sold for the prince, nor a single sheaf of the whole grain harvest on any single acre of the Bogucharovo fields.

Alpatych, arriving from the devastated Bald Hills estate, sent for Dron on the day of the prince's funeral and told him to have twelve horses readied for the princess's carriages and eighteen carts for the belongings to be moved from Bogucharovo. Though the peasants paid rent, Alpatych expected no difficulty with this order, since there were two hundred and thirty households at work in Bogucharovo and the peasants were well-off. But on hearing the order, Dron lowered his eyes and said nothing. Alpatych named certain peasants he knew, from whom he told Dron to take the carts.

Dron replied that those peasants' horses were away carting. Alpatych named others, but they too, according to Dron, had no horses available: some were carting for the government, others were too weak, and others had died for lack of fodder. It seemed that no horses could be found even for the carriages, let alone for the carting.

Alpatych looked hard at Dron and frowned. Just as Dron was a model village Elder, so Alpatych had not managed the prince's estates for twenty years in vain. He was a model steward, possessing to the highest degree the ability to read the needs and instincts of those he dealt with. Having glanced at Dron, he immediately understood that the Elder's answers did not reflect his personal views but the general mood of the Bogucharovo commune, which had already carried Dron along with it. But he also knew that Dron, who had acquired property and was hated by the commune, must be torn between two camps: the masters' and the serfs'. He saw this hesitation in Dron's eyes and therefore frowned and stepped closer.

"Now listen, Dronushka," he said. "Don't talk nonsense to me. His excellency Prince Andrew himself gave me orders to move all the people away and not leave them for the enemy, and there's an order from the Tsar about it too. Anyone who stays is a traitor to the Tsar. Do you hear?"
"I hear," Dron answered without lifting his eyes.
Alpatych was not satisfied with this reply.
"Look, Dron, things will end badly!" he said, shaking his head.
"The power is in your hands," Dron replied sadly.

"Listen, Dron, drop this!" Alpatych repeated, withdrawing his hand from his coat front and solemnly pointing to the floor at Dron's feet. "I can see through you—and three yards into the ground under you," he continued, staring at the floor before Dron.
Dron was unsettled, glanced furtively at Alpatych, and lowered his eyes again.

"Drop this nonsense and tell the people to get ready to leave their homes for Moscow, and have carts ready by tomorrow morning for the princess's things. And don't go to any meeting yourself, do you hear?"
Dron suddenly fell to his knees.
"Yakov Alpatych, let me go! Take the keys from me and let me go, for Christ's sake!"

"Stop that!" cried Alpatych sternly. "I see through you and three yards under you," he repeated, knowing that his skill in beekeeping, his knowledge of the right time to sow the oats, and the fact that he had kept the old prince's favor for twenty years had long since earned him a reputation as a wizard, and that the power to see three yards underground is considered an attribute of wizards.
Dron got up and was about to say something, but Alpatych interrupted him.
"What have you all got into your heads, eh?... What are you thinking?"
"What am I supposed to do with the people?" said Dron. "They're completely out of control. I've already told them..."
"'Told them,' I'm sure!" said Alpatych. "Are they drinking?" he asked abruptly.
"Completely out of control, Yakov Alpatych; they've brought in another barrel."
"Well then, listen! I'll go to the police officer, and you tell them so, and that they must stop all this and have the carts ready."
"I understand."

Alpatych did not press further. He had managed people long enough to know that the main way to make them obey is to show no suspicion that they might disobey. Having wrung a submissive "I understand" from Dron, Alpatych left it at that, though he not only doubted but felt almost certain that without military help the carts would not be forthcoming.

And so it was: when evening came, no carts had appeared. In the village, outside the tavern, another meeting was being held, and it was decided to drive the horses into the forest and not provide the carts. Without saying anything about this to the princess, Alpatych had his own belongings taken from the carts that had come from Bald Hills and had those horses harnessed instead for the princess's carriages. Meanwhile he went himself to the police authorities.
